clue.text: Make, say, a vain attempt to nobble "The Weakest Link"

definitions.meaning: to make for is to go for, and the target is the jugular, a vein, which sounds like 'vain': a 'vein attempt'
to attack the most vulnerable point, as a predator goes for the throat

explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is cryptic: 'make' is an example of going for something, and the jugular is a vein, punned on as 'vain'. The Weakest Link was a British TV quiz show.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to attack an opponent ruthlessly at their most vulnerable spot.

clue.text: Wallenstein his s-spine-tingler

parts.note: the stuttered opening gives a lone S
a spine-tingler is a chiller, a frightening tale

explanation.surface: A stammering comment about the playwright's Wallenstein being a thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wallenstein his' is the old way of writing 'Wallenstein's', i.e. the author of Wallenstein; the stammer supplies the extra S.
explanation.definitionFit: The German dramatist wrote the Wallenstein trilogy of plays, so he is its author.

clue.text: Lamb departs before she cooks it?

indicators.note: the departure letter is placed in front of the essayist

parts.note: d. is the abbreviation for departs in timetables
Charles Lamb wrote his essays under the pen name Elia

explanation.surface: A lamb is taken away before a woman roasts it.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb looks like meat for the oven; it is the essayist Charles Lamb. Delia Smith is a famous British TV cook.
explanation.definitionFit: Delia Smith is Britain's best-known cookery writer, so the name is an example of a woman who cooks.

clue.text: Guinness collection perhaps included "Sally"

indicators.note: one word is taken into the middle of the other

parts.note: Guinness is a famous stout
an art collection, so 'collection' suggests art

explanation.surface: A Guinness record collection featured a woman named Sally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sally' looks like a woman's name; it is the verb meaning to set off, as in sally forth.
explanation.definitionFit: To sally is to set off or venture forth on a journey or excursion.

clue.text: Firmly wears the breeches, then 'e holds your britches as an alternative

definitions.text: Firmly wears the breeches, then 'e holds your britches as an alternative

parts.words: Firmly wears the breeches, then 'e holds your britches as an alternative
parts.note: someone who wears the breeches is in charge, and holding another person by their britches (... shorts) is a joking variant of the coarse idiom for total control

explanation.walkthrough: To wear the breeches (or trousers) is to be the boss; the clue plays on the idiom for having someone completely in your power, with britches as shorts.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means having someone utterly at your mercy and under your control.

clue.text: Talent broken reed spent

parts.note: a knack is a talent or skill

indicators.note: the reed is broken up and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A gifted musician's broken reed is used up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' turns REED into ERED. 'Knackered' is British slang for exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, being worn out or exhausted is to be knackered, the same as spent.

clue.text: Holiday in the can

parts.note: the jazz singer surnamed Holiday had this first name, which also sounds like the camper's cooking can

explanation.walkthrough: Billie Holiday was the American jazz singer; a billycan is a metal can for cooking over a campfire.
explanation.definitionFit: Billie Holiday's first name, sounding like the billycan used for brewing tea outdoors.

clue.text: See 5
Pit workers with soldiers joining revolutionary's art movement

parts.note: OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers
Che Guevara is the archetypal revolutionary, so Che's

indicators.note: the word art is set in motion and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Miners, aided by troops, join a revolutionary's artistic movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pit workers' suggests miners; an orchestra plays in the orchestra pit. 'movement' makes TRA from ART.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre musicians play in the orchestra pit, so they are workers in the pit.

clue.text: Sound horse? On the contrary, no sound

indicators.note: a word that sounds like 'no' in old speech

parts.note: nay is an old word for no

explanation.surface: Is the horse sound? Quite the opposite, no it isn't.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' flips 'sound horse' into 'horse sound', the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A neigh is the sound a horse makes, so a horse sound, the clue's reversed phrase.

clue.text: Actor with heart of gold and one rival

indicators.note: the central letters of gold are taken

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
a vier is one who vies, a rival

explanation.surface: An actor with a heart of gold and a single rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurence Olivier was the great English stage and film actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Olivier is one of the most celebrated actors of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Society's impressed by one magnifying view on bussing

indicators.note: the letter is pressed inside the eyepiece word

parts.note: an ocular is the eyepiece of a microscope or telescope
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: Society is impressed by a magnified view of bus travel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bussing' suggests transport; a buss is a kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to kissing, and to buss is an old word for kiss.

clue.text: The duty of the sexton?

parts.note: a duty is a levy or charge, and the sexton's job is ringing the church bell

explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a tax or charge and the slow ringing of a bell, which a sexton does.
explanation.definitionFit: A toll is a duty or charge, and also the bell-ringing that a church sexton performs.

clue.text: Develop characters, say, with a Spanish wordsmith

indicators.note: the letters of develop are its characters, reshaped

parts.note: e.g. means for example, i.e. say

explanation.surface: To develop characters, as a Spanish writer does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' turns DEVELOP into LOPEDEV. Lope de Vega was a prolific Spanish playwright of the Golden Age.
explanation.definitionFit: Lope de Vega was a hugely prolific Spanish dramatist and poet, so a wordsmith.

clue.text: Actor wrapped up with one the French had

indicators.note: the word is mixed up and its letters reordered

parts.note: draped means wrapped in cloth
one is I, the Roman numeral
eu is the French past participle of avoir, to have

explanation.surface: An actor bundled up with someone the French had.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DRAPED into DEPARD. Gérard Depardieu is the French film actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Gérard Depardieu is one of France's best-known film stars.

clue.text: Grave robber's introduction into undead East End rabble

indicators.note: the robber's initial goes inside the rearranged letters
a rabble is a disorderly crowd, so the letters are jumbled
un-dead: the D, an abbreviation for dead, is removed
the first letter of robber's is taken

explanation.surface: A grave robber gets into a crowd of zombies in London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' looks like part of 'grave robber' but is the definition. Removing D from EAST END leaves EASTEN, which 'rabble' rearranges round R.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave and earnest both mean serious and solemn in manner.

clue.text: Elemental prophet and emperor, one and the same externally

indicators.note: the first pieces sit outside the emperor

parts.note: one is A, the indefinite article
id. (idem) is Latin for the same
Nero was a Roman emperor

explanation.surface: A prophet and an emperor, outwardly one and the same.
explanation.walkthrough: An aneroid barometer forecasts the weather, hence a prophet of the elements.
explanation.definitionFit: An aneroid barometer predicts the weather, making it a forecaster of the elements.

clue.text: Romance left abandoned in the wheat

indicators.note: wild and unrestrained, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A love affair left forsaken in the wheat field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned' looks like 'left behind' but is the anagram signal for ROMANCE plus L.
explanation.definitionFit: Amelcorn is another name for emmer, an old variety of wheat.

clue.text: Rode down naked? O, all right!

parts.note: naked means open or undisguised, i.e. overt
OK means all right

explanation.surface: A rider coming down naked? Oh, fine then!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rode down' suggests descending on horseback; here it means caught up with and passed.
explanation.definitionFit: To ride someone down is to catch up with them, so to overtake them.

clue.text: Beyond one's remit to reconcile true rivals

indicators.note: rivals reconciled are rearranged into harmony

explanation.surface: It is beyond one's authority to make peace between true rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin legal phrase means beyond one's powers.
explanation.definitionFit: The legal Latin phrase means acting beyond the powers or authority granted to one.

clue.text: Storm centre that's part of the service

definitions.meaning: a storm in a ... is a fuss over nothing, so the cup is where the storm is
one item of a tea service

explanation.walkthrough: A storm in a teacup is the idiom for a big fuss about something trivial.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'storm in a teacup' places a storm there, and a cup is part of a tea set.

clue.text: Time to conclude home study mark

indicators.note: the time letter is placed at the end

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
a den is a study

explanation.surface: Time to finish the home study course with a mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mark' here is an impression or notch.
explanation.definitionFit: An indent is a mark or impression pressed into a surface.

clue.text: An admirer of cockney belles, do we hear?

indicators.note: asks whether the word is heard as another

parts.note: a true cockney is born within the sound of Bow bells, the bells of St Mary-le-Bow in London

explanation.surface: Is an admirer of cockney belles mentioned?
explanation.walkthrough: 'belles' puns on 'bells': the famous bells are Bow bells, and Bow sounds like the word for a suitor.
explanation.definitionFit: A beau is a boyfriend or male admirer.

clue.text: See 5
Self-reliant girl died sadly

parts.note: Una is a girl's name

indicators.note: sadly, i.e. badly, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl who looked after herself died a sad death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' turns DIED into IDED.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something unaided means doing it alone, relying on yourself.

clue.text: Radio detector in the maze of television

definitions.meaning: an early radio receiver used a mineral as its detector
The ... Maze was a British TV game show

explanation.walkthrough: The Crystal Maze was a popular British TV game show; crystal sets were early radios.
explanation.definitionFit: A crystal served as the detector in early radio sets, and named a TV maze show.

clue.text: Rate Ben Adam's bearing

parts.note: Abou (Abu) Ben Adhem is the title figure of Leigh Hunt's poem, so Abu belongs with Ben Adam
SE, south-east, is a compass bearing

explanation.surface: Rate the bearing of Ben Adam.
explanation.walkthrough: To rate someone, in its old sense, is to scold them.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate someone is to berate or scold them, which is a form of verbal abuse.

clue.text: Hardly a hot tip for the highest objective?

definitions.text: Hardly a hot tip for the highest objective?

parts.words: Hardly a hot tip for the highest objective?
parts.note: the top of the globe is the coldest of destinations, the ultimate goal of polar explorers

explanation.walkthrough: The top of the world is a freezing spot and was the goal of polar explorers.
explanation.definitionFit: The northernmost point of the Earth is both the top of the globe and frozen.
